title: Selecting and installing a water butt pump
subtitle: Choosing between submersible and inline pumps for low-pressure rainwater distribution
excerpt: A gravity-fed water butt delivers about 0.3 litres per second, fine for a single watering can fill, too slow for a hosepipe or drip irrigation system. A small submersible pump in the butt raises the flow rate to 10 to 15 litres per minute, enough to run a soaker hose around the kitchen garden. This tutorial covers pump selection, installation, and the common mistakes that shorten pump life.
sourceNotes: WRAS (Water Regulations Advisory Scheme) guidance on non-mains water use in gardens. Garden pump manufacturer technical specifications (Hozelock, Gardena, Karcher). RHS watering guidance 2024.

glossaryTerms.definition: The pressure a pump can produce, measured in metres of water column (m). A pump with 3 m of head can push water 3 m vertically. For horizontal runs, 10 m of pipe length is roughly equivalent to 1 m of head due to friction.
A pump designed to operate while fully submerged in the water source. Pulls water from around it and pushes it through a hose or pipe. Common in water butts and ponds.

content.text: A water butt without a pump is limited by gravity. The maximum flow rate depends on the height of water above the tap, typically 500 to 800 mm in a standard 210-litre butt, giving a gravity flow of around 0.3 to 0.5 litres per second at the tap. This fills a 10-litre watering can in 20 to 30 seconds. To run a soaker hose or a drip system serving more than a couple of raised beds, a pump is needed.

For a standard garden water butt application (up to 30 m of soaker hose, or filling watering cans), a basic submersible garden pump rated at 3,000 to 4,000 litres per hour is sufficient. Key specifications to check:

Maximum flow rate at zero head, the flow when pushing water horizontally with no height to overcome. A 3,500 l/h pump gives approximately 58 litres per minute, or 0.97 litres per second, about twice a hosepipe's useful rate.

, the maximum height the pump can raise water to. For a butt at ground level feeding a raised planter 1 m above: you need 1 m of head plus a margin. A pump rated at 3 m head is sufficient for most garden layouts.

Particle size, the pump should tolerate particles up to 3 mm. Water butts collect windborne debris, small insects, and algae. A pump without a filter or with a 1 mm strainer will block in the first season.
into the butt on a length of rope or wire tied to the handle. The pump should rest at the bottom of the butt and pull water from around the strainer.

Fit the outlet hose to the pump discharge, typically a standard 1/2" or 3/4" push-fit hose barb. Run the hose out through or over the butt lid. If running through the butt wall, drill a 20 mm hole above the high water mark and seal with a grommet.

Route the electrical cable over the butt rim. Use a weatherproof outdoor socket (IP44 rated) on a 2.5 mm cable run to the nearest socket. The pump circuit should be protected by an RCD. Never use an indoor extension lead from a window to a garden pump.
Test with the butt full, run the pump for 2 minutes and check for leaks at all fittings.

In autumn, remove the pump before the first hard frost. Rinse the strainer, flush the hose, and store the pump in a frost-free location. A pump left submerged through a freeze cycle, particularly if the butt cracks or the water level drops below the pump body, is likely to fail. A quality garden pump lasts 3 to 5 seasons with this care; without it, one winter.
